body.text: Xi Jinping's India visit marked managed competition, not reconciliation. Both nations seek mechanisms to control rivalry and avoid escalation. India emphasizes mutual respect and boundary settlement, while China seeks stability. Diplomatic and economic ties offer cautious optimism for future engagement. Sustained peace and political dialogue are key for durable relations.

Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the 18th BRICS Summit marks an important, if carefully calibrated, moment in India-China relations. His first visit to India in seven years, since the 2019 informal summit at Mamallapuram, comes after a prolonged period of military confrontation, diplomatic estrangement and strategic mistrust following the 2020 Galwan Valley clash. The significance of the visit lies less in any dramatic breakthrough than in the fact that both Beijing and New Delhi now appear willing to stabilise a relationship that had become increasingly defined by confrontation.

Xi held a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the summit, hosted under India’s chairmanship with the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” China will assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027, ensuring another institutional opportunity for sustained engagement.

The 2020 Galwan clash fundamentally altered the trajectory of bilateral relations. The deaths of 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers triggered a prolonged military standoff along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), accompanied by suspended flights, reduced people-to-people contacts and a sharp decline in political engagement. India subsequently imposed restrictions on Chinese applications and tightened scrutiny of Chinese investments, reflecting growing concerns over economic and technological vulnerabilities.

For several years, the relationship settled into an uneasy equilibrium in which military deployments and infrastructure development continued along the border while high-level political engagement remained limited. The October 2024 patrolling agreement provided the first significant opening. Modi-Xi interactions at the 2024 Kazan BRICS summit and later in Tianjin, combined with renewed Special Representatives’ talks involving National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, gradually created the conditions for the present visit.
India subsequently imposed restrictions on Chinese applications and tightened scrutiny of Chinese investments, reflecting growing concerns over economic and technological vulnerabilities.

The important point is that neither side has abandoned its fundamental strategic assessment of the other. Rather, India and China are attempting to establish mechanisms through which competition can be managed without repeatedly escalating into crisis.

The language surrounding the Modi-Xi meeting is revealing. Both leaders stressed the need for a strategic and long-term perspective and argued that India and China should regard each other as partners rather than rivals or threats. The central proposition was that differences should not automatically become disputes.

For Xi, this approach reflects Beijing’s broader interest in stabilising its external environment. China faces uncertainty over trade, supply chains, relations with the United States and instability in several regions. Xi therefore emphasised calibrating perceptions, leveraging each country’s strengths for development, supporting each other’s BRICS presidencies and coordinating in institutions such as the UN, SCO and G20. His call for India and China to remain “good neighbours and friends” reflects Beijing’s preference for managing differences while preserving space for cooperation.

Modi, however, framed the relationship around India’s established principles of mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest. For New Delhi, normalisation cannot be separated from peace and tranquillity along the border. Modi’s emphasis on a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable boundary settlement underlined that economic and multilateral cooperation cannot indefinitely substitute for progress on the LAC.

India’s reaffirmation of its positions on Taiwan and Tibet, along with its assurance that Indian territory would not be used for anti-China activities, also served as a signal of reassurance. New Delhi appears willing to acknowledge Chinese sensitivities, but expects reciprocal restraint and stability from Beijing.

The discussions covered trade, investment, the border and broader efforts to stabilise relations. The objective of the meeting was not to resolve the India-China relationship, but to make it more manageable.

The visit offers several reasons for cautious optimism. First is diplomatic normalisation. Xi’s return to India, the ceremonial welcome and renewed leader-level dialogue represent the clearest evidence since Galwan that the two sides are moving away from prolonged diplomatic paralysis. Regular political contact can reduce misperceptions and create channels for managing future crises.

Second, there is an economic opportunity. India cannot completely insulate its growth trajectory from China, one of the world’s largest economies and a major component of global supply chains. Greater trade, investment and people-to-people contacts could ease some of the frictions that have accumulated since 2020. But progress will depend on Beijing addressing Indian concerns over market access, investment restrictions and the trade imbalance.

Third, the broader geopolitical environment creates incentives for selective cooperation. Uncertainty surrounding US trade policy under Donald Trump, tensions in West Asia and vulnerabilities in global supply chains provide areas where Indian and Chinese interests may overlap. Such cooperation should not be interpreted as strategic convergence; it reflects pragmatic alignment where interests coincide.

The BRICS framework is particularly useful in this regard. It offers India and China a multilateral space for engagement without requiring them to align on the broader international order. India prefers BRICS to remain a broad platform for the Global South rather than an explicitly anti-Western bloc, while China is more willing to use it to challenge Western dominance. Their approaches remain different, but continued interaction within BRICS serves both countries.

The limits of the rapprochement are equally important. The core boundary dispute remains unresolved, military deployments and infrastructure development continue, and strategic mistrust has not disappeared. India and China continue to compete across the Indo-Pacific, technology, the Global South and the neighbourhood.

Economic relations also remain complicated. While interdependence creates incentives for cooperation, India remains concerned about excessive dependence on Chinese supply chains and technology. Security considerations will therefore continue to shape economic policy.

The differences over BRICS reflect a larger strategic divergence. India seeks a multipolar order that allows it to work simultaneously with the United States, Russia, China and other partners. China increasingly seeks an international environment less dominated by the United States. These competing visions will constrain the depth of India-China cooperation even when tactical interests overlap.

The current thaw should therefore be understood as managed competition rather than reconciliation. Both countries have recognised that uncontrolled deterioration carries significant costs, but neither has fundamentally altered its strategic posture.

Xi Jinping’s visit is best seen as a milestone in the post-Galwan stabilisation process, not as a reset of India-China relations. It demonstrates that both sides are prepared to invest political capital in preventing strategic competition from becoming permanent confrontation.

The durability of this process will depend on what follows the summit optics. Three factors will be decisive: sustained peace along the LAC, concrete progress on economic and people-to-people ties, and continued high-level political engagement.

India and China are unlikely to become close strategic partners in the foreseeable future. Their interests overlap in some areas and collide in others. New Delhi’s objective should therefore not be to eliminate competition with Beijing, but to ensure that competition remains bounded, predictable and manageable.

The present moment is consequently best described as stabilisation without strategic trust, engagement without reconciliation, and cooperation without convergence. That may appear modest, but given the trajectory of bilateral relations since 2020, it represents meaningful progress. The real test will be whether this diplomatic thaw can survive the next crisis-and whether it can gradually produce a more stable modus vivendi between two increasingly consequential Indo-Pacific powers.
This commentary originally appeared in The Economic Times.
